item.title: Mike Johnson's message to House Republicans: Show up for work
item.description: “Barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our two year term,” he said.

media:content.media:title: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) holds a media availability at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Speaker Mike Johnson is urging full attendance from House Republicans during the final month of the GOP trifecta, after leaders had to cut this past legislative workweek short because not enough members were in Washington to pass party-line legislation.

“Over the next 44 days, we need every House Republican to remain fully engaged so we can get even more of our important priorities signed into law,” Johnson (R-La.) said in a letter to colleagues Friday morning.

“To state the obvious,” he added, “barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our two year term.”

The House GOP’s razor-thin majority has taken a major hit post-midterms, where defeated incumbents are feeling little incentive to trek to Washington when they’ll be out of office come January: Of the 14 Republican members who missed votes Wednesday, 11 will not be returning next year, prompting leadership to pull plans to hold a party-line procedural vote that would have failed.

In his letter, which he posted on X, Johnson noted several bills the House is working with the Senate to finish, including an annual defense policy package, government funding legislation and a permitting overhaul measure that the Senate passed late Thursday night.

GOP leaders have also floated taking up a college sports bill when they return from the Thanksgiving holiday.

“To do all of this,” Johnson said, “we must have full attendance and the support of our entire conference.”

item.title: Don’t let employees auto-delete messages, top House Democrat warns DOJ, DHS
item.description: Rep. Jamie Raskin urged law enforcement officials to ensure employees are preserving government records.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) speaks with reporters outside the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 14, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney
item.content:encoded:
A top House Democrat says he’s received evidence that federal law enforcement officials have been destroying work-related communications by using personal messaging apps like Signal, equipped with auto-delete functions.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, slated to lead the House Judiciary Committee in January, is urging the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security to ensure that their employees — and officials at subagencies including the FBI, ICE and the Bureau of Prisons — are taking steps to preserve their messages ahead of the Democratic takeover of Congress.

In letters he sent to law enforcement officials Wednesday, Raskin appended a screenshot of what appears to be a work-related, set-to-delete Signal conversation with FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer.

“The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records,” Raskin wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications.”

Federal laws require government employees to preserve their official communications, even those sent on personal devices or via messaging services like Signal, WhatsApp, Telegram and other commonly used apps.

The Maryland Democrat described the exchange as “one of many” that had been reported to the committee, raising concerns about more systematic destruction of communications Democrats intend to seek when they lead investigations next year. He is asking Justice Department officials to take steps to recover any deleted messages by scouring for backups or “associated metadata.”

Similar letters were sent to the FBI, ICE and the Bureau of Prisons.

A spokesperson for the Justice Department said in a statement that the agency "follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions. The men and women of the DOJ who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated by a congressman who once called 2020 riots ‘magnificent’ and ‘nonviolent.'"

Spokespeople for DHS, FBI, ICE and the Bureau of Prisons didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Trump administration has indicated that it is unlikely to give much credence to demands made by lawmakers before they formally wield committee gavels. White House counsel Will Scharf wrote to House Democrats on Wednesday underscoring that the administration will refuse oversight demands from members of the minority party — a policy adopted in Trump’s first administration and later embraced by Joe Biden’s White House.

item.title: Ro Khanna wants to lead Democrats on China policy. He’s not alone.
item.description: The California lawmaker is banking on his party leaders reinstating a panel that would give him a major platform ahead of 2028.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is angling to lead the House Select Committee on China in the next congress and become the Democrats' dominant voice on how Washington should navigate ties with Beijing.

item.dc:creator: By Phelim Kine, Ari Hawkins and Kelsey Brugger
item.dc:contributor: By Phelim Kine, Ari Hawkins and Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
As he eyes a presidential run in 2028, Rep. Ro Khanna is trying to carve out a role as Democrats’ premier voice on China policy. And he’s bullish he will have a platform to do that on Capitol Hill, despite a brewing turf war over who will lead on an issue drawing headlines thanks to Nvidia’s chip-smuggling scandal.

In an interview Thursday, the California lawmaker said he was confident that House Democratic leaders would revive the select committee on China that the outgoing GOP majority created in 2023 — and on which he has served as the top Democrat since January.

“I believe we will have the committee,” he said, adding that it’s now a question of “the title and the exact jurisdiction.”

Asked if he thought Democrats might turn it into a subcommittee housed within the Foreign Affairs Committee, Khanna said, “My guess is that it’ll stay an independent committee, but we’re having those conversations.”

Incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries hasn’t committed to preserving the select committee, saying at a press conference this week “it’s a conversation that we’ll have” after the caucus finishes picking its leaders for the next Congress. A Jeffries aide said in an email Thursday that “vigorous oversight of China-related matters will be an important priority next Congress regardless of committee structure.”

But the stakes are high for Khanna as he waits for official word of whether the Select China Committee will be reinstated. While he has long fashioned himself as an expert on the region and related policies, the panel’s gavel would give him a megaphone to promote his vision — plus paint a sharp contrast not only with President Donald Trump and his GOP successor on the 2028 ticket, but also with fellow Democrats competing in the party’s primary.

“Jeffries has made me the ranking member for a reason,” Khanna said in a separate interview before the midterms. “We are going to articulate this new policy from this committee.”

A former Khanna staffer pointed out that the committee’s largely symbolic role

makes it an ideal messaging platform — one that would let Khanna hone and refine his messaging on Trump and the economy. The panel has no power to advance legislation, just hold hearings and make recommendations.

“This can be a testing ground,” said that former aide, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their old boss. “He needs the practice.”

Khanna’s plans could be dashed, however, as internal politics come into play. Some fellow Democrats are openly questioning whether the committee is still necessary at all, especially amid the party’s power sweep that has members jockeying for influence.

The turf war on Asia policy is in particular heating up as U.S.-China rivalry over artificial intelligence draws new attention on Capitol Hill.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster over his ties to a suspected Chinese spy involved in an alleged chip smuggling scheme has set off bipartisan alarm about Beijing’s access to advanced U.S. chips and America’s standing in the AI race, and it has also sharpened worries about national security.

”I'm very concerned with the Nvidia chips,” Khanna said Thursday. Regarding Trump, he added, “I mean, how do you go to China and not be direct with [Chinese leader] Xi Jinping that they are stealing our chips? … Our president should say, ‘absolutely, never again,’ that ‘we will not stand for our chips being stolen.’”

With lawmakers across parties and chambers now pushing new restrictions on foreign sales of advanced AI chips and demanding answers from Huang and the Trump administration, multiple Democrats are positioning to lead the response.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the likely chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee next year, said he would defer to Jeffries but emphasized his panel was already well-positioned to tackle issues related to China.

“I do believe that we have the wherewithal to follow those issues within the committee, as had been done in the past,” he said in an interview Thursday. “So I'm ready, willing, and able if that's what he wants me to do … with individuals who are on the committee that have the expertise to deal with it and who won't skip a beat. And I think that we'll then have even additional authority that a task force will not have.”

Rep. Ami Bera (D-Calif.), who will likely take the gavel of the Foreign Affairs subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific in January, wants other committees to take back the China portfolio.

“It doesn't make sense to keep the Select Committee on China — certainly in the last two years it has been less relevant,” he said earlier this month.

Bera isn’t alone in wanting to pull the plug on the committee. Rep. Johnny Olszewski (D-Md.), who serves on the subcommittee on East Asia, said in a recent statement the larger Foreign Affairs Committee is “well positioned to provide that oversight and hold the administration accountable for its China policy.”

The China committee’s defenders disagree.

“The notion of shutting down the China Select Committee—for no reason other than internal turf battles and institutional egos—is simply inexplicable,” said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y) in a statement earlier this month.

There’s support for the committee’s continuance on the other side of the aisle, as well, with the current chair, John Moolenaar of Michigan, saying the panel has been “a force multiplier” in bringing out “the best of each of these committees of jurisdiction” now competing for influence.

Khanna insisted in the pre-midterm interview that any role he plays on the China committee in the next Congress “will have nothing to do” with a possible presidential run or bolstering his own standing.

But losing his perch there would make it harder to get his voice heard on the issue, as other possible 2028 Democrats jostle for primacy on foreign affairs. Rahm Emanuel, former President Joe Biden’s ambassador to Japan, is offering a competing vision for U.S.-China policy.

In an interview with POLITICO last month, Emanuel argued that the next president should focus on exploiting China’s “domestic vulnerabilities,” including pressure on what he calls the “shambles” of the Chinese economy.

“I think parts of the party — and it's not just the left —have been intellectually lazy and politically timid” in their approach to China, Emanuel added.

Khanna has cast himself as a generational antidote to what he sees as the compromises and passivity of senior Democratic leadership, declaring himself “not a Chuck Schumer Democrat” in recent speeches.

He also assails the China policies of the 1990s under both GOP and Democratic administrations defined by what he calls “total engagement and capitulation” to Beijing, while promising to steer a course away from “the total decoupling and isolationism that happened under Trump.”

That may not be enough for some members of Democrats’ ascendent left, who have called for a more conciliatory approach to China’s Communist government. Incoming New York Rep. Claire Valdez, one of six members of the Democratic Socialists of America who won House seats earlier this month, has called for an end to a “cold war posture” toward Beijing and a reduction in U.S. military bases overseas.

Khanna has tried to strike a balance between hawks and doves by declaring China a “strategic competitor,” emphasizing engagement over confrontation and pitching an industrial policy that can both sharpen America’s technological edge against Beijing and create jobs.

Yet on Thursday, he downplayed any tension within his party or the House caucus, saying that he has “great respect” for Meeks and that they enjoy “a very cordial and collaborative relationship.”

He also predicted that they will continue to work together — as committee chairs.

“It will be a similar subject area,” Khanna said of the select committee. “The question is, what will be the exact title? We're working on that.”

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

item.title: Capitol agenda: Dems draft a curb on Iran war cash
item.description: A group of Democrats are closing in on a proposal to cut off Iran war funding as part of a spending deal that would avert a government shutdown in three weeks.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) speaks with reporters at the U.S. Capitol on July 27, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
A group of Democrats is closing in on a proposal to cut off Iran war funding as part of a spending deal that would avert a government shutdown in three weeks.

The main tenets they’re circling: No cash for offensive actions unless President Donald Trump gets war authorization from Congress with a clear exception for defensive operations in the face of enemy attack.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) said Thursday night a group of Senate Democrats has finalized a draft of the proposal, telling us, “I think we’ve gotten agreement.”

There are miles to go before this becomes a workable deal. The group still has to circulate it to the entire caucus, which Kaine said he was not sure would happen Friday, and there are no bipartisan leadership talks currently underway. Lawmakers have until Dec. 11 to avoid a funding lapse.

Notably, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) didn’t shoot down the idea and questioned if Democrats would trade the Iran restrictions for more national security money and munitions replenishment.

“I think if you could fence off Iran and do some of the other stuff we need to do, I think that’s a conversation we’d be interested in,” Thune said in an interview Thursday.

Thune’s comments come after Kaine told us Democrats were “starting to test” Republicans about what it might take to reach a deal. Kaine also floated a trade-off of war restrictions for munition funding.

Sens. Chris Coons of Delaware, Patty Murray of Washington, Jack Reed of Rhode Island, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Mark Warner of Virginia are also in the group of Senate Democrats formulating a plan, according to a person familiar with the discussions.

Such a trade-off could appease Democrats who may want to cut off Iran war funding but don’t want to risk triggering a shutdown to do it. It could also please defense hawks who were worried about low munition inventory but don’t want to bless the Trump administration’s year-end defense funding demand with its soaring $350 billion price tag.

What else we’re watching:

— NORTH CAROLINA FRESHMEN FEEL 2028 PRESSURE: North Carolina’s new House Democrats know they’re on borrowed time — and they’re determined to govern like it. No crop of incoming freshmen in the new Democratic majority arrived under more shocking circumstances than the band of relatively unknown political newbies who defeated some of the state’s most prominent Republicans — including Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the House Republican campaign arm. Now these lawmakers-elect are under a shot clock to prove to their new constituents they can deliver where Republicans could not — and their success could determine Democrats’ future prospects in an increasingly purple state.

— PERMITTING BILL HEADS TO HOUSE: Senators on Thursday night passed in a 62-33 vote a landmark permitting reform bill, sending it to the House where support from both parties is more hazy. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told POLITICO on Wednesday he would try to pass the bill under expedited procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority and bars floor amendments. If that effort fails, he said he would bring it up under a standard rules procedure requiring a simple majority.

Jordain Carney, Jennifer Scholtes, Katherine Tully-McManus, Nico Portuondo and Anthony Cruz contributed to this report.

item.title: Tillis to block Trump’s comptroller general pick from confirmation in year-end package
item.description: The North Carolina Republican’s hold could doom the nominee’s chances.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is approached by reporters as he arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Thom Tillis plans to block the speedy confirmation of White House aide Eric Ueland to head the Government Accountability Office by opposing his inclusion in a catchall nomination package Senate Republicans plan to approve next month.

The North Carolina Republican's opposition substantially diminishes the chances Ueland will be confirmed as comptroller general in the waning days of GOP control of Congress.

“I’ve already issued a presumptive hold if it comes out of committee,” Tillis said in an interview Thursday night regarding Ueland’s nomination. “I won't allow him to go through en bloc.”

Tillis and several other Republican senators have raised concerns that Ueland would not be able to objectively lead the independent oversight agency in his capacity as a close Trump ally currently serving as a top official at the Office of Management and Budget.

While Tillis said he thinks Ueland “is an honorable guy,” he predicts it would be difficult for the nominee to resist giving in to directives from Trump administration officials, including White House budget director Russ Vought.

“I just can't imagine that he could withstand the pressure that would come from the people that put him there and the relationships he has,” Tillis said of Ueland. “I think we need somebody more independent for that office to have credibility.”

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chair Rand Paul said his panel — which held a hearing on Ueland’s confirmation Thursday morning — is likely to vote to approve the nomination the day senators return to Washington after the Thanksgiving holiday.

Paul has not publicly endorsed the nomination, but the Kentucky Republican said in a brief interview Thursday night that he has “no intention of opposing him.”

item.title: Elissa Slotkin backs Van Hollen's leader bid
item.description: The Michigan senator said voters don't want "nibbling at the edges."

media:content.media:title: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 23, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin said Thursday she will back Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader over longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. She had previously announced opposition to Schumer but had not committed to any alternative.

“Because I’ve been clear that I won’t be supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen,” Slotkin said in a video announcement.

Schumer acknowledged Slotkin last year as a rising star in the Democratic Party when he selected her to deliver their party’s response to President Donald Trump’s joint address to Congress. Since Van Hollen made his bid for majority leader official earlier this month, Slotkin had been on the sidelines, claiming any candidate needed to present a vision for the party’s first 100 days in power.

In the video, Slotkin compared the need for transition in the Senate Democratic ranks to the situation after she first was elected to the House in 2018 and longtime leader Nancy Pelosi was seeking a return to power. Under pressure from some younger members, Pelosi ultimately stepped down from leadership after two additional terms as speaker.

“The American public spoke loud and clear about what they wanted to see in the country and from this new generation of leadership,” Slotkin said. “Not marginal change. Not small nibbling at the edges.”

Van Hollen’s list of public supporters remains in the single digits, with Slotkin becoming the fifth caucus member to announce they will vote for him. The Maryland senator has said he has around 15 public and private commitments, short of the 28 needed in addition to his own vote.

item.title: House Ethics revamps rules in effort to streamline sexual misconduct probes
item.description: The panel is grappling to improve its response after facing a wave of sexual misconduct investigations of lawmakers this year.

media:content.media:title: House Ethics Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) prepare to convene a hearing on Capitol Hill on April 21, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
The House Ethics Committee voted unanimously Thursday to change its internal rules as it aims to expedite sexual misconduct probes.

The panel, which operates largely in secret, has been under pressure to increase its transparency and streamline its investigations into lawmaker behavior after a spike in sexual misconduct claims this year.

Lawmakers on the panel adopted one rule change that formalizes a long-standing practice to publicly disclose when a member is found to have engaged in sexual harassment while ensuring victims’ and witnesses’ identities are protected.

Another change adopted allows the panel’s chair and ranking member to issue subpoenas, bypassing the need to hold a full committee vote. Panel members would still receive notification about the authorization of subpoenas.

A third change “expands when fines and denials of privileges are appropriate sanctions” for sexual misconduct, according to Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.). The change aims to ensure lawmakers are held more accountable for their actions.

“We believe these rule changes will provide more transparency and they will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for victims, while also making sure that due process is protected for the members themselves,” Guest said.

Another change adopted formalizes a requirement that the Ethics panel review its rules and make necessary adjustments each Congress.

The updates come as lawmakers — including bipartisan duo Reps. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.) and Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) — continue to craft legislation to make sweeping changes to how the House polices bad behavior.

“All of these changes just go to reinforcing our commitment to the integrity of the House of Representatives,” said ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.). “On sexual harassment, all of us agree on zero tolerance, and we’re going to be clear about that.”

item.title: Tim Scott open to joint Bessent-Lutnick testimony on Nvidia fallout
item.description: Adding Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to the hearing would set up a remarkable public airing of the Trump administration’s differing views.

media:content.media:title: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, left, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent attend a welcome ceremony for President Donald Trump in Manila, Philippines, Nov. 18, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Michael Stratford
item.content:encoded:
Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Thursday he is open to calling Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to testify alongside Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick next month as the two Cabinet secretaries feud over chip exports to China in the wake of the Nvidia espionage scandal.

Lutnick, who has drawn Republican criticism for his handling of artificial intelligence chip exports, has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in early December after Scott requested his public testimony. Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to appear at separate hearing before the panel.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) asked Scott at a nominations hearing Thursday whether the panel could invite Bessent to testify alongside Lutnick and Jeffrey Kessler, who leads Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security.

“Happy to do so,” Scott responded. “They should be here in early December.”

It's not clear whether Scott plans to move ahead with a formal invitation to Bessent. His spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment.

Kennedy said he wanted to “get them all three here together” before the committee. Questioning an unrelated Treasury Department nominee, Kennedy asked: “Why is the Department of Treasury allowing our Department of Commerce to allow China to circumvent our export controls on advanced chips?”

Adding Bessent to the hearing with Lutnick would set up a remarkable public airing of the Trump administration’s differing views on how to approach China’s desire to obtain advanced U.S. technology needed to compete on AI. The two men accompanied President Donald Trump on his trip to China this week.

Bessent has publicly pointed the finger at Lutnick’s Commerce Department for failing to put Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that purchased advanced Nvidia chips, on a trade blacklist amid reports of its apparent ties to China.

Earlier this week, Bessent directed a new Commerce Department rule cutting off Chinese companies’ ability to remotely access advanced AI chips from Nvidia in Southeast Asian data centers. The Commerce Department said the rule was “written by and at the direction” of Bessent’s Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council.

item.title: Trump’s CISA nominee dodges questions on who won the 2020 election and whether Jan. 6 was an insurrection
item.description: Michael LoSapio told lawmakers that he plans to reevaluate CISA’s budget and staffing if confirmed.

media:content.media:title: During a confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee, Michael LoSapio sidestepped questions about thorny issues between the Trump administration and CISA.

item.dc:creator: By Maggie Miller
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency refused to give a clear answer on who won the 2020 election and whether the events of Jan. 6, 2021, constituted an attack on the U.S. Capitol when questioned by lawmakers Thursday.

During a confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee featuring several other nominees, Michael LoSapio, currently the chief information security officer at Palantir, sidestepped questions about his perspective on thorny issues between the Trump administration and CISA.

The cyber defense agency has historically supported nationwide efforts to secure U.S. elections and came under fire in 2021 for saying the elections were “the most secure in American history,” despite Trump’s unsubstantiated claims that the results were rigged.

Over the last year, the Trump administration has significantly scaled back CISA’s election security efforts and urged the agency to focus on core missions, such as protecting critical infrastructure and providing cybersecurity support to federal agencies.

“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said when Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) asked for his thoughts on who won the 2020 election. “My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States.”

Blumenthal accused LoSapio of “ducking the question … in a way that betrays your lack of independence and objectivity” and said he was “disqualified from the position you have been nominated to fill.”

In another exchange with the senator, LoSapio said he did not believe the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection was an attack on the U.S. Capitol.

“I wasn’t involved in politics” at the time, he replied.

LoSapio’s responses seem to have tanked his confirmation odds. A spokesperson for Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) — who will retire in January — confirmed to POLITICO on Thursday that he plans to place a hold on LoSapio's nomination. While the spokesperson did not give a reason, Punchbowl News reported that Tillis is blocking LoSapio because of his comments on the Jan. 6 insurrection.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) is also placing a hold on LoSapio's nomination, telling POLITICO in a statement, "you can’t have an insurrectionist Palantir executive in charge of our nation’s cybersecurity and election security."

Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.) criticized the events of Jan. 6 but defended LoSapio’s responses.

“It was big, it was huge and it shouldn't be excused, it should be criticized,” Paul said during the hearing. “It was some attack, some riot, but it was also some people, and some of these people got locked up … that weren’t violent.”

A spokesperson for committee ranking member Gary Peters (D-Mich.) did not immediately respond to a request for comment on LoSapio’s responses.

The committee must vote on LoSapio’s nomination before the full Senate can. Paul told reporters after the hearing that he anticipates the committee will vote on LoSapio “in early December.”

CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since January 2025, when former Director Jen Easterly stepped down. Trump previously nominated former Energy Department and Coast Guard official Sean Plankey for the role, but Plankey withdrew his nomination in April after it failed to advance in the Senate.

LoSapio would be coming into the role as the agency is rebounding from a series of layoffs and budget cuts that led to the agency losing about one-third of its staff last year.

When asked how he would approach agency staffing, LoSapio said he would “get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis.”

Gregory Svirnovskiy contributed to this report.

item.title: Bipartisan trio unveils new AI safety framework
item.description: Reps. Sara Jacobs, Celeste Maloy and Don Beyer will lead the legislative effort.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.) takes part in a town hall discussion on Feb. 23, 2026, in Washington, D.C.

item.dc:creator: By Owen Dahlkamp and Gabby Miller
item.dc:contributor: By Owen Dahlkamp and Gabby Miller
item.content:encoded:
A bipartisan trio of House members unveiled a sweeping framework for a frontier artificial intelligence safety bill on Thursday that would create federal safety rules for the industry.

It comes as lawmakers grapple with how to regulate the industry while still encouraging development. It also comes as Democrats lay the groundwork for AI policy next Congress.

The legislation, referred to as the Safe and Accountable Federal Evaluations of Artificial Intelligence, or SAFE AI Act, would impose transparency requirements, create guidance for independent evaluators and lay out an enforcement regime. Reps. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.), Celeste Maloy (R-Utah) and Don Beyer (D-Va.) are leading the effort.

POLITICO first reported details of the framework last month.

“No industry gets to police itself, and AI shouldn’t be the exception,” Jacobs said in a statement, saying the trio’s proposal is a “floor — not a ceiling.”

Maloy, in a statement, underlined how the proposal “leaves room for Utah and other states to set safeguards of their own.” The move is meant to appease Democrats who have broadly opposed a GOP effort to preempt state AI laws.

Some tech companies argue that a patchwork of state laws is difficult to comply with. Safety groups, meanwhile, broadly think that states should be allowed to craft regulations that are stricter than the federal government.

It joins other bipartisan legislative efforts this Congress, including the FRONTIER Act, introduced by Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), that attempt to define the federal government’s role in overseeing the emerging technology.

The new bill would impose civil penalties on companies that violate safety frameworks that AI developers would be required to publish. Trahan released a liability proposal last month following concern about who would be held responsible if rogue AI agents wreak havoc on the virtual or physical world.

The measure also wants to use independent evaluators as a mechanism for government oversight, but with strict guidance on which third-party verifiers can evaluate developers and their models.

Similar provisions have been backed by major tech companies, including OpenAI, though safety groups have raised concerns that evaluators directly paid by AI labs may not be able to offer independent assessments.

The proposal would also empower judges to require mitigation measures for AI systems when requested by the government and create whistleblower protections for AI lab employees speaking out about safety concerns.

item.title: House Democrats round out leadership roster
item.description: Reps. Maxwell Frost, Sarah McBride and Sydney Kamlager-Dove won the only contested race.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) arrives for the House Democratic Caucus leadership elections on Capitol Hill on Nov. 18, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats filled out their leadership team Thursday, elevating a diverse slate of lawmakers to run the caucus next term.

Reps. Maxwell Frost of Florida, Sarah McBride of Delaware and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of Californmia won the only contested slots, to be co-chairs of the House Democrats’ policy and communications arm known as the DPCC, receiving 195, 238, and 180 votes respectively. That left out a fourth candidate, Rep. Eric Sorensen of Illinois, according to a person with knowledge granted anonymity to share the private tally.

“Our messaging was united and unifying, and that's what got us the majority,” Kamlager-Dove said in an interview after the vote. “And now people want a continuation of that, so I'm hopeful that I'll be able to help push for greater tools, greater access, and the ability to truly connect with the American people.”

In uncontested races, House Democrats elected Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan to serve another term as DPCC chair. They also picked Rep. Morgan McGarvey of Kentucky as caucus leadership representative and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan as battleground leadership representative.

The newly incoming members elected Reps.-elect Dan Koh of Massachusetts, Donna Miller of Illinois and Fred Wellman of Missouri as freshman class co-presidents. They picked Reps.-elect Daniel Biss of Illinois and Jessica Killin of Colorado as freshman representatives to the Steering and Policy Committee. They also selected Reps.-elect Christina Bohannan of Iowa and Jasmine Clark of Georgia as freshman representatives to leadership.

On Wednesday, Democrats nominated top leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker. He is set to be officially elected on the House floor in January.

The caucus also picked Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Rep. Pete Aguilar of California as whip, Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker, Rep. Ted Lieu of California as caucus chair and Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois as caucus vice chair.

item.title: Trump's top watchdog pick vows to investigate the White House he now serves
item.description: The president is trying to get one of his top aides confirmed to a 15-year term as comptroller general before Democrats take control of Congress.

media:content.media:title: Eric Ueland testifies before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Capitol Hill, Sept. 12, 2017, in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump's nominee to be the federal government's top watchdog, told senators Thursday that "a hallmark" of his tenure as head of the Government Accountability Office would be investigating the White House — where he currently works as a top official.

“My role and responsibility is to call it as I see it, and that is exactly what I will do if I have a privilege,” Ueland told the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee during his confirmation hearing. “We will fully follow through on charges from Congress.”

It was part of Ueland's effort Thursday morning to assuage concerns that he would be anything other than nonpartisan and unbiased if confirmed to serve a 15-year term as comptroller general and head of GAO, after the nomination of the veteran GOP congressional aide and White House official has sparking concerns among members of both parties.

Democrats are expected to band together to oppose Ueland primarily because he currently serves as a top official at the Office of Management and Budget, which has been at the forefront of withholding and canceling federal dollars Congress has approved. Now the president is pushing for his confirmation — in the final weeks before Republicans surrenders their majority to Democrats — to lead the one agency uniquely empowered to sue the Trump administration over its funding moves.

During his confirmation hearing, Ueland said the Constitution grants Congress “a significant power of purse and responsibility for stewarding those resources provided by taxpayers.”

“The job of the Comptroller General and the GAO in this area,” he added, “is to make sure that all information is available — that all applicable laws are applied — and when questions about the conduct of the executive branch arise, provide information to Congress and this committee. And that's what I think we have to continue to do.”

But Ueland’s work at OMB “undercuts any credibility he could possibly have to lead the GAO,” said the committee's top Democrat, Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan — because the White House budget office under Trump “routinely flouts congressional oversight, has stonewalled GAO audits and defied Congress' constitutional authority to direct spending.”

Ueland has also been serving as acting director in charge of the U.S. Agency for International Development the Trump administration has worked to disband, prompting ongoing lawsuits challenging the legality of shuttering what used to be the world's largest foreign aid agency.

“The American people expect a whole lot more from Congress than just a rubber stamp for the president,” Peters said. "Someone with his partisan record deserves more scrutiny, not less. These actions are embarrassing."

Democratic opposition means Ueland will need to focus on shoring up support among Senate Republicans, specifically those uneasy about seating a White House ally atop the federal oversight agency responsible for defending Congress against executive branch overreach.

There are also concerns about the manner in which he was nominated. At the White House’s request, Republican lawmakers included Ueland on a list of recommendations they sent Trump this month. But they did not stand up a bipartisan panel, as required by law, to search for and suggest candidates.

It was only after Trump had “already decided” on Ueland that Republican lawmakers gave their Democratic counterparts less than 24 hours to submit recommendations for the role, Peters said.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), who chairs the committee in charge of vetting Ueland's nomination, said Thursday that Democrats had almost a year to submit recommendations for Trump’s nomination to head GAO and, “they did nothing. They submitted no names.”

Paul did not express support for Ueland, nor did he reveal whether he will vote to approve the nominee for floor consideration. He said in a brief interview Thursday afternoon that the panel will likely hold a vote on Ueland the Monday after the Thanksgiving holiday.

Some GOP senators have already expressed reservations about Ueland’s nomination after Trump announced his selection earlier in the week, including Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Sen. John Curtis of Utah.

Sen. James Lankford said during the hearing that while it appears the White House followed “the letter of the law” in nominating Ueland, “I’m not sure they followed the entire spirit of the law.” But the Oklahoma Republican added that he thinks Ueland is "a great candidate" for the role.

Before serving in prominent roles in Trump’s second administration, Ueland was a top Senate staffer who then brokered pandemic relief negotiations on Capitol Hill as a White House aide during the president’s first term.

Until late last year, GAO was headed by Gene Dodaro, an accountant who began his career at the agency and was confirmed as its head in 2010. His retirement in December sparked early worries among Democrats that Trump would seize the opportunity to nominate a replacement who would not challenge the administration.

Since Dodaro's departure, Orice Williams Brown has been serving as acting comptroller general, where she's been under under increased pressure from Democrats and Republicans to sue the Trump administration for withholding federal cash.

Aside from probing the executive branch’s funding moves, GAO audits government programs. At the request of congressional committees, the agency also launches investigations and provides recommendations for saving taxpayer dollars.

item.title: New bipartisan AI caucus forms with two dozen House members
item.description: The group will be chaired by Reps. George Whitesides, Don Beyer and Nathaniel Moran.

media:content.media:title: Rep. George Whitesides, then Virgin Galactic CEO, watches as his former company's carrier aircraft flies over Spaceport America near Upham, New Mexico, on Aug. 15, 2019.

item.dc:creator: By Owen Dahlkamp
item.content:encoded:
A bipartisan coalition of over two dozen House lawmakers is forming a new artificial intelligence caucus.

The group, dubbed the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, will be led by Reps. George Whitesides (D-Calif.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas). It will seek to balance creating AI safeguards that mitigate the technology’s risks with “ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies,” according to an announcement first shared with POLITICO.

The group’s creation comes as lawmakers look ahead to the next Congress and grapple with Washington's role in governing the emerging technology.

“We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides, who is positioning himself as a prominent voice on AI in Congress, said in an interview.

He said the group would work to create, give feedback on and endorse legislation. Other groups tend to focus more on educating members or working on legislation with colleagues of their own party, leaving a gap for a bipartisan coalition like his.

They would also make a concerted effort to engage in “rapid response” to AI incidents and breaches, which other caucuses have been less engaged in, he said. When incidents occur and the public questions whether to attribute it to AI, like the outage of major infrastructure that Americans experienced the past week in the country’s air traffic control systems or Microsoft Outlook, the group will leverage their contacts across industry, safety groups, the intelligence community and other government agencies to gather information.

“We want to begin to communicate to the American public that Congress can move at a pace that is responsive to the pace of AI change,” said Whitesides, a former chief of staff at NASA.

Whitesides’ push is joining a crowded field of other AI-focused bodies that have formed in Congress.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries formed an AI commission chaired by three Democrats tasked with charting the caucus’ future on AI policy.

The Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus, co-chaired by four lawmakers, including Beyer, has been focused on educating members on the technology, Whitesides said. In contrast, his group will try to take a more active voice in tech policy on the Hill.

Democrats have also debated creating a select committee on AI. But the idea has faced opposition from some lawmakers poised to chair committees that oversee AI policy,

The trio of chairs will be joined by California Democrats Sara Jacobs, Ro Khanna, Sam Liccardo, Ted Lieu, Zoe Lofgren, Brad Sherman, Doris Matsui and Scott Peters alongside Greg Casar (D-Texas), Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), Ben Cline (R-Va.), Mike Flood (R-Neb.), Bill Foster (D-Ill.), Valerie Foushee (D-N.C.), Pat Harrigan (R-N.C.), Jim Himes (D-Conn.), Mike Kennedy (R-Utah), April McClain Delaney (D-Md.), Blake Moore (R-Utah), Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.).

item.title: Raskin eyes Judiciary Committee probe of Trump ‘pardon brokers’
item.description: The incoming chair said he is hiring “a few dozen” staffers to pursue a range of investigative targets.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) speaks with reporters outside the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 11, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney
item.content:encoded:
Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee, said Thursday he expects to use his power to investigate President Donald Trump’s pardons once he and fellow Democrats take the majority next year.

Presidential pardons, a historically tricky subject to legislate on given the president’s “unilateral” constitutional authority, nevertheless warrant a deep dive, Raskin told reporters.

A House probe, he said, could look into the new world of “pardon brokers,” intermediaries who have used their access to the Trump White House to help well-connected figures secure pardons. He also said the committee could explore whether anti-bribery laws should be freshened to include this new cottage industry.

“The president's pardon power certainly doesn't extend to people who aren't president, and there are a lot of people who are now involved in this new industry,” he said. “So we're going to, you know, pull the covers back and see exactly what's going on.”

Raskin said he anticipates hiring “a few dozen” new staffers to bolster the wide range of investigations he expects his panel to pursue. Many of them, he said, will be drawn from the ranks of former prosecutors fired in a purge of Justice Department officials who worked on probes related to Trump, the Jan. 6 Capitol attack and other matters disfavored by the president.

To crack down on pardons, Raskin said the committee could explore whether to make people who lobby for pardons register as “pardon agents” in a manner similar to the way agents of foreign governments are required to register.

“There’s a lot that can be done,” he said.

Lauren Bis, a a White House spokesperson said anyone who is “spending money to lobby for pardons is foolishly wasting their money."

"The Trump Administration has a robust pardon review process which includes White House counsel, the Department of Justice, Pardon Czar Alice Johnson, and ultimately, the President himself as the final decider,” she said.

item.title: Capitol agenda: GOP trifecta sputters into final days
item.description: Some GOP lawmakers openly wonder what their party will get done before the end of the year under renewed pressure from the White House to ram through a swath of stalled priorities.

media:content.media:title: From left, Sens. James Lankford (R-Okla.), John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), and John Thune (R-S.D.) look on during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Republicans wanted to check off a list of policy goals before Democrats took over Congress. They’re hitting some major hurdles instead.

Senate Republicans emerged from hours of meetings Wednesday without a clear path to advance another party-line spending bill. Chances have also dimmed on confirming some of President Donald Trump’s executive branch nominees.

And House Republicans, unable to even proceed through regular floor business due to attendance issues, have cut their legislative workweek short.

It’s all left some GOP lawmakers openly wondering what their party will get done before the end of the year under renewed pressure from the White House to ram through a swath of stalled priorities.

“I don’t know if we’re going to do anything,” Sen. John Kennedy said of his chamber, except confirm judges. “But everything else, I have no idea what we’re going to do.”

Here’s where the major agenda items stand:

— RECONCILIATION 3.0: Senate Republicans insist they aren’t closing the door on another party-line bill, but many are skeptical it will come together.

Even if it does in the Senate, House GOP leaders are unlikely to have the votes to adopt it given how many members are MIA after losing their elections.

— YEAR-END STAPLES: GOP appropriators made the case during their closed-door meeting Wednesday to hold off on reconciliation for now to allow government funding negotiations to proceed, several senators said after the meeting. Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed as much but declined to say how much time Republicans would give the bipartisan government funding talks.

Lawmakers appear far from consensus on government funding as the Dec. 11 shutdown deadline approaches. Also waiting for floor action: the annual defense policy bill and the farm bill.

— TRUMP’S NOMS: Committees have until Dec. 1 to advance any nominee they want to have included in a bloc of Trump picks set to be confirmed en masse next month, but there are signs of GOP pushback against some nominations that could keep them out of the package.

The White House also surprised senators by pulling Heidi Overton to lead the FDA, and other nominations have hit snags.

What else we’re watching: 

— SCHUMER'S LAST STAND? While Chuck Schumer fights to remain Democratic leader in the Senate, a big question remains about what he’ll do in two years. Schumer’s Senate term expires in 2028, and interviews with Democrats in New York and Washington suggest that moment could mark the end of his accomplished career one way or another. Some believe he will retire, and others are urging him to. Otherwise, they warn, he risks a bruising, potentially career-ending primary. In a statement responding to questions about his future, Schumer touted his record of delivering billions of dollars for New York through decades of challenges — like 9/11 and Covid.
 
— FINAL SENATE PERMITTING STRETCH? Senators will try again Thursday to pass a landmark bipartisan permitting reform deal after two Democrats Wednesday held up the legislation aimed at streamlining energy projects. Negotiators will now look to resolve outstanding disagreements and secure a timing deal for amendment votes and final passage as soon as Thursday. Sens. Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley did not consent to a time agreement necessary for lawmakers to proceed to amendment votes Wednesday, spokespeople for their offices confirmed.

Jennifer Scholtes, Jordain Carney, Mia McCarthy, Chris Sommerfeldt and Nico Portuondo contributed to this report.

item.title: A US attorney warned Dems about their Trump rhetoric. Legal experts say ignore him.
item.description: A Texas prosecutor says lawmakers’ plans for aggressive oversight could cross a criminal line.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Robert Garcia, who is slated to chair the House Oversight Committee, was one of five Democratic lawmakers who received letters.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney
item.content:encoded:
A federal prosecutor says he’s pre-investigating potential future crimes by Democratic lawmakers who might one day abuse their oversight powers.

The notion is so farcical it should simply be ignored, say six experts in congressional power and constitutional law.

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, the Trump-appointed top prosecutor in south Texas, sent letters to four senators and a House member — all Democrats expected to wield powerful gavels in January — suggesting that their vows to aggressively investigate President Donald Trump’s allies could lead to criminal probes and charges.

Veterans of executive-legislative clashes say Reitz’s letters are legally meritless. There’s simply no crime, they say, when a member of Congress describes possible future oversight actions — even aggressive or controversial ones. And when they take the majority, those lawmakers’ investigative actions would be protected by one of the most powerful immunities in government: the Constitution’s speech or debate clause.

“They’re saber-rattling, but there’s no force behind the saber,” said Stan Brand, a former House general counsel under Speaker Tip O’Neill, who said Democrats should disregard the letters and avoid “adding a patina of legitimacy to what is essentially crackpot legal practice.”

Reitz’s letters to the five lawmakers — Sens. Elissa Slotkin, Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthaland Adam Schiff, as well as Rep. Robert Garcia — have raised eyebrows in Washington for the suggestion that lawmakers’ pre-election comments about investigating Trump allies could amount to criminal intimidation.

Democrats targeted by Reitz have vowed to push forward with their investigations and reject his attempt to criminalize what they say are their constitutional rights and duties. On Wednesday, Slotkin in a post on social media urged him to “bring it on."

"If there's a legal case to be made that you should prosecute someone for freedom of speech, do it. Come get me," Slotkin said in a video.

The Justice Department has stood by Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz and aide to outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, defending the substance of his letters.

“Oversight is not a license to threaten private citizens for exercising their First Amendment rights,” the Justice Department said in a statement that cited the same criminal statute referenced by Reitz. “Congress gave DOJ the authority to investigate those who willfully deprive people of their constitutional rights.”

But legal experts say the Hill shouldn’t sweat it.

“I’d largely ignore it and not give it air,” said one white collar attorney who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he previously represented Trump allies. A second attorney who has been active in congressional oversight matters said the latest spate of attacks from the White House and Justice Department is “even more laughable than usual.”

“Congress has extremely broad latitude to conduct oversight of the executive branch, and … the Speech or Debate Clause provides Congress, its committees, its members, and its staff (when functioning at the direction of the members) with a shield against any executive branch efforts to impede that oversight,” said Steven Huefner, an Ohio State University law professor who spent five years in the office of the Senate’s legal counsel from 1995-2000. “I therefore think that Congress can ignore the recent threats.”

Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown University law professor, said Reitz’s letters are “so clumsy and over the top” that they would be unlikely to provoke a serious legal clash between the branches. He said serious challenges to Congress’ authority are likely to develop later, once Democrats begin exercising their oversight power.

“It has seemed inevitable since long before Election Day that the Trump administration would take an incredibly combative approach against any efforts on Congress’s part to exercise even traditional forms of oversight over the executive branch,” Vladeck said. “The odds that, somewhere along the way, that approach provokes novel and serious Speech or Debate Clause issues seem as high as the odds that they’ll provoke novel questions about executive privilege, Congress’s legitimate investigative powers, and everything in between.”

Reitz said in a statement Tuesday that he’s simply following “the facts and law” by sending letters that ask lawmakers to preserve relevant documents.

After a left-leaning group filed a bar complaint against him this week, Reitz vowed to “continue my preliminary inquiry unfazed: to determine whether certain members of Congress have unlawfully stepped outside the legitimate legislative purpose of their planned committee activities, and to ensure Americans’ constitutional rights are protected.”

At the heart of the administration’s position are two longstanding principles: All congressional investigations and subpoenas must be tethered to a “legitimate legislative purpose,” and the Constitution’s speech or debate clause — intended to protect lawmakers from intimidation or coercion from the executive branch — applies only to a “narrow” slice of core legislative activity and not to broader conduct by lawmakers, like media interviews or subpoenas issued for improper purposes.

“I have taken routine, pre-investigatory steps to conduct a preliminary inquiry into certain members of congress for their statements vowing to weaponize committee activities against private citizens and entities associated with President Trump,” Reitz said in a statement, describing his letters as being sent “in coordination with Main Justice.”

A Justice Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the department’s internal deliberations, said there was nothing amiss about Reitz’s pre-review of potential oversight abuses.

“Sending threatening letters to Americans for associating with the President — before those officials have oversight power — is a clear attempt to chill associational rights and speech,” the official said. “And, yes, it is a valid exercise of DOJ’s prosecutorial power to prevent ‘anyone acting under the color of law to willfully deprive a person of their constitutional or federal rights.’”

Reitz’s letters have gotten some public backup from Trent McCotter, the Department of Justice’s second-in-command, who echoed the claim that the senators’ comments could violate Trump allies’ First Amendment rights. “DOJ will defend against threats to those rights,” McCotter wrote on X.

Reitz’s letters followed a similar missive from White House counsel Will Scharf to Rep. Robert Garcia, who is slated to lead the House Oversight Committee in January. Scharf’s letter borrowed language from a federal criminal statute to warn the California Democrat against aggressive investigations.

“[T]hreats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality,” Scharf wrote.

Though constitutional law experts say DOJ’s position is unlikely to clip Congress’ oversight ambitions, the battle for public opinion is another matter. Trump, they noted, has effectively countered congressional probes and impeachment efforts by pointing to Democrats’ own commentary and casting the investigations as “lawfare” or “weaponization” against him and his allies.

Through that lens, the attacks from the White House and Justice Department could be more effective. The administration’s letters point to loose comments from incoming House Democrats about raining down subpoenas like “Mardi Gras beads” or imploring Trump allies to “lawyer up.” Garcia jokingly described his future oversight plans as the result of “pettiness,” a comment that Scharf and Reitz both seized on.

Those comments could cost Democrats public support, some experts say, and also form the backbone of the administration’s litigation strategy against subpoenas they claim are not tied to a “legitimate legislative purpose.”

But the messaging fight is unlikely to translate into legal victories, they say. Though courts have paid attention to stray comments from Democrats during previous investigations, they have almost uniformly affirmed Congress’ broad power to obtain information.

So long as lawmakers embrace a plausible legislative purpose for their probes, “it is not a court’s ‘function’ to invalidate a congressional investigation,’” U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden wrote in 2021, ruling in favor of a House effort to obtain Trump’s tax returns.

McFadden, a Trump appointee, acknowledged comments from top Democrats, like House Ways and Means Chair Richard Neal and then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, had muddied the picture, but the judge said even mixed motivations are not enough to undercut Congress’ power.

That principle has held in more than a century of battles between the branches, during which courts —including the Supreme Court — have repeatedly held that the motives of individual members simply can’t overcome the will of the House or a legislative committee when pursuing a legislative goal.

“I wouldn’t dignify this with some counteroffensive in court,” Brand said of Congress’ response to the Trump administration letters. “If these guys try to enforce, it’s going to get flushed.”

item.title: The Republican trifecta is sputtering in its final days
item.description: Thin margins, attendance issues and stalled negotiations are adding up to a challenging lame-duck session.

media:content.media:title: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (right) and other top Republicans have yet to commit to attempting a costly GOP-only spending bill.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes, Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.dc:contributor: By Jennifer Scholtes, Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Republicans want to run through the tape in their final weeks in power on Capitol Hill, but they’re hitting some major hurdles.

With 17 working days left in the Senate before Democrats take charge, Republicans emerged from hours of meetings Wednesday without a clear path to advance a party-line spending bill the White House desperately wants — just as several of President Donald Trump’s nominees hit snags that threaten to keep key roles filled by acting officials for two years.

House Republicans, meanwhile, are simply spinning their wheels. Leaders announced Wednesday they would cut their workweek short because of attendance issues.

It’s left some GOP lawmakers openly wondering what their party will get done before the end of the year beyond seating more Trump-appointed judges and, they hope, averting a government shutdown. The Senate is aiming to pass a bipartisan permitting reform bill this week, but it faces a more uncertain path in the House, which is also sitting on a bipartisan college sports bill the Senate passed months ago.

“I don’t know if we’re going to do anything,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said after emerging from one of the Senate GOP’s closed-door meetings Wednesday. “I think we’re going to continue to confirm judges, I’m pretty sure of that. But everything else, I have no idea what we’re going to do.”

Across the Capitol, one House Republican granted anonymity to speak candidly said there are “very low odds” Republicans will be able to enact any bill through the filibuster-skirting reconciliation process — especially given how many members have stopped coming to work after bruising election defeats.

“It’s dereliction of duty,” the Republican said, adding leaders would need to “publicly shame” colleagues “by name” into showing up.

The reality check comes as House and Senate Republicans have been under renewed pressure from the White House to use the waning days of their governing trifecta to ram through a swath of stalled GOP priorities.

As they met and reelected their leadership team after the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, Senate Republicans agreed to a nonbinding resolution saying they would seek to "maximize" their remaining time in power — including confirming every possible nominee, passing “core” GOP priorities and attempting another reconciliation bill.

The party-line bill, in particular, is easier said than done. Trump has demanded $350 billion in military spending be included because Democrats are dead-set against supporting any funding that could further the war with Iran.

But many GOP senators, while publicly supportive, have long been privately skeptical it will come together. For one thing, Republicans still haven’t fully agreed on the scope of the hypothetical measure — $350 billion is more than many budget hawks can stomach.

For another, the Senate math gets harder for the GOP next month when incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio is sworn in after winning a special election to finish out the term of Vice President JD Vance, lowering the GOP’s majority to 52.

“Everybody recognizes it's going to be a herculean effort to try to get the House and the Senate to agree on the scope and the process,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said Wednesday.

Besides the GOP-only bill, legislators also need to worry about advancing three other typically bipartisan year-end staples: the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill and a measure to fund the government past a looming Dec. 11 funding deadline.

GOP appropriators made the case during their closed-door meeting Wednesday to hold off on reconciliation for now to allow government funding negotiations to proceed, several senators said after the meeting. Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed as much but declined to say how much time Republicans would give the bipartisan government funding talks.

Republican senators are also discussing whether to bring a spending package to the floor that would combine two fiscal 2027 bills: one funding veterans affairs and another funding the Pentagon, according to three GOP senators and aides granted anonymity to describe private conversations.

But Democratic votes will be needed to make this tactic work — and Democrats are not likely to support bankrolling the Pentagon without Iran restrictions and a guarantee that nondefense programs would get a funding increase, too.

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) said it would put Democrats on the spot: “Are they willing to work with us or not? And this makes them answer that question.”

Republicans are having success confirming Trump’s judicial nominees, with some vowing not to leave town this week until they have cleared a batch that has been teed up for votes. But some of the president’s other nominees are facing less certain prospects.

Committees have until Dec. 1 to advance any nominee they want to have included in a bloc of Trump picks set to be confirmed en masse next month. But there are signs of GOP pushback against the nominations of Eric Ueland to head the Government Accountability Office and Kari Lake to be ambassador to Jamaica, among others, that could keep them out of the package.

The White House also surprised senators by pulling Heidi Overton to lead the FDA, and HELP Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) declined to move forward with a top science nominee who was supposed to get a committee vote.

Republican leaders were also struggling to get things done in the House this week, with leaders unable to begin floor debate on two GOP-sponsored bills after 14 House Republicans didn’t show up to vote Wednesday. Eleven were nonreturning members.

Those attendance problems aren’t expected to get better: Outgoing House members had to vacate their offices and relocate to cubicles this week, further demoralizing defeated GOP incumbents who would just as soon close out their terms back home.

The upshot is that House GOP leaders are unlikely to have the votes to adopt any reconciliation measure that comes over from the Senate. Most House Republicans wanted the Senate to take up a framework they passed before the midterms instead.

House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas), for instance, threw cold water on the likelihood of approving Trump’s full $350 billion defense request.

“I don't believe that you can win over enough budget hawks,” he said in an interview. “That’s my concern.”

Calen Razor and Katherine Tully-McManus contributed to this report.

item.title: GOP Rep. Nick Begich survives blue wave
item.description: The Alaska Republican hung on even as the GOP lost a Senate race and the governorship.

media:content.media:title: Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich is the sponsor of a bill that would blacklist foreign fishing vessels that illegally fish in U.S. waters.

item.dc:creator: By Lisa Kashinsky
item.content:encoded:
GOP Rep. Nick Begich III fended off an independent candidate who had the backing of the Democratic apparatus to hold onto Alaska’s sole House seat — becoming one of the rare Republicans facing a serious challenger to survive the party’s midterm bloodbath.

Begich, who aligned himself with Donald Trump despite the president’s unpopularity, narrowly prevailed over Bill Hill and two other candidates after a ranked-choice tabulation Wednesday, even as Democrats flipped other statewide offices in reliably red Alaska.

He’ll serve next year alongside former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democrat he defeated to win the House seat just two years ago, after she ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The scion of a prominent Alaska political family also succeeded in a year that saw his uncle, Democrat Tom Begich, drop out of the governor’s race after finishing second in the August primary to consolidate support behind another Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who went on to win the governorship.

Hill, meanwhile, extends independent candidates’ midterm losing streak, joining a number of independent Senate candidates who lost red-state races to Republicans this year. House Democrats’ campaign arm had added the educator and commercial fisherman to its coveted “Red to Blue” program. But Eric Hafner, a perennial candidate who is serving a prison sentence in New York, was the sole Democrat listed on the ballot and still siphoned votes.

Democrats have won 257 seats to 172 for the GOP, with a half-dozen races left to be called.

item.title: Laurel Lee makes bid for top Republican on House Judiciary Committee
item.description: The Florida Republican is a former prosecutor and judge.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Laurel Lee (R-Fla.) departs a House Republican Conference meeting at the Capitol Hill Club in Washington, Sept. 18, 2024.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Laurel Lee has formally announced her bid Wednesday to lead Republicans on the House Judiciary Committee — a position that would have her going head-to-head with Democrats who could decide they want to impeach President Donald Trump.

“I understand the constitutional grounds for impeachment, the limits of congressional authority, and the difference between a policy disagreement and an impeachable offense,” said the Florida Republican in a letter to colleagues, obtained by POLITICO. “I am prepared to make those distinctions in the hearing room and explain them to the public.”

In her letter, Lee highlights her experience as a judge, federal prosecutor and Florida secretary of state to make the case that she can “distinguish allegations from evidence, apply the law fairly, and explain consequential decisions clearly.”

She also told her colleagues that she would be well-equipped to combat the wide range of investigations that committee Democrats — led by incoming Chair Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) — are already telegraphing.

If recommended for the post by the House GOP Steering Committee, Lee, who was elected to Congress in 2022, would be among the few Republican women in leadership roles in the chamber. She is expected to be competing against Reps. Lance Gooden (R-Texas) and Scott Fitzgerald (R-Wis.) for the position.

item.title: Van Hollen calls for AI safeguards amid leadership push
item.description: Failure to address AI risks would replicate the mistakes of the 1990s, the Maryland Democrat said.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks during the Senate Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies hearing on Capitol Hill on May 12.

item.dc:creator: By Sam Sutton
item.content:encoded:
SAUSALITO, California — Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said that setting guardrails around artificial intelligence would be a top priority if he succeeds in his challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats next year.

“The bottom line here is, we can’t take the same attitude toward AI that too many people took to Big Tech in the 1990s, which is that: ‘It’s inevitable. It’s out of our control,’” he said during a remote “fireside chat” at a Hewlett Foundation event. “That is a bunch of nonsense.”

The severity of AI-related cybersecurity risks, along with its rapid emergence as a driving force of economic growth in the U.S., has hastened calls for incoming Democrats majorities to move swiftly to head off potential threats. In his remarks, Van Hollen said that AI companies must “understand they’re going to be fully liable for any harm they cause” — even in instances where rogue agents fail to cause material harm. He also cited workforce-related issues as a concern.

“In a democracy, all of us should help develop the rules that help nourish our communities, and not simply allow it to go to folks who are trying to make a big, big buck,” he said.

In addition to targeting large AI firms, Van Hollen also said that he would prioritize policies targeting the role of private equity in youth sports, health care and the acquisition of small businesses. He also said that lawmakers should “go after” surveillance pricing techniques.

Schumer addressed AI risks himself Wednesday, lambasting President Donald Trump and his administration for not acting more decisively in light of the recent disruptions to critical digital infrastructure.

“We need to ensure the safe development and deployment of AI, or we’re going to see more outages and, God forbid, even catastrophic events going forward,” he said in a floor speech.

item.title: Lauren Underwood elected vice chair of House Democratic Caucus
item.description: The 40-year-old former Health and Human Services official beat California Rep. Sara Jacobs.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.) arrives for a press conference at the U.S. Capitol, Nov. 19, 2024.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois was elected vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus Wednesday, beating Rep. Sara Jacobs of California in a rare contested leadership race, 143-118.

Underwood, 40, is currently a co-chair of the caucus’ policy and communication arm and has served in leadership roles with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

She campaigned for the vice chair post leaning on her experience previously serving as a frontline member who flipped a Republican-held suburban Chicago seat in 2018. She boasted strong fundraising numbers and vowed to lead on Democratic messaging.

The vice chair position is effectively No. 6 on the Democratic leadership ladder. Races for the higher rungs were all uncontested.

item.title: Republican senator cancels vote on Trump pick to lead science foundation
item.description: Bill Cassidy said National Science Foundation nominee Jim O'Neill "did not do enough to stand up for science" as a Trump health official.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) canceled a vote for President Donald Trump's nominee to run the National Science Foundation.

item.dc:creator: By Chelsea Harvey
item.content:encoded:
The Republican chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee canceled a vote scheduled for Wednesday morning on Jim O’Neill’s nomination to lead the National Science Foundation, saying the former health official failed to stand up to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

O’Neill, a former government health official, would have been the first NSF director without a scientific or engineering background, which drew opposition from Democrats and science advocacy groups.

Committee Chair Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) cited O'Neill's stint as acting director of the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from August 2025 to February in canceling the nomination vote. “As acting CDC director, Mr. O’Neill did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from Secretary Kennedy,” Cassidy said.

Cassidy also said O'Neill's role in firing the CDC's director, Dr. Susan Monarez, for failing to support Kennedy's questionable vaccine policies "raised further concerns about the independent judgment he would bring to NSF.”

“I like Jim personally,” Cassidy added. “But this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right.”

The scientific community widely opposed O’Neill’s nomination, citing his lack of scientific experience, his ties to Silicon Valley and his CDC record.

The nonprofit Stand Up for Science said it facilitated more than 1,000 calls and emails to Cassidy opposing O’Neill’s nomination in the past two days.

Gretchen Goldman, president of the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists, said Tuesday that “NSF needs to be led by someone who can champion science for the public good and Jim O’Neill is not that person.”

The cancellation came after the HELP Committee had declined to hold a confirmation hearing for O’Neill, prompting Democratic senators to push to delay the vote on his nomination.

Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) sent a letter to Cassidy on Tuesday arguing that “the Senate should have an opportunity to hear directly from the nominee about how he would lead NSF.”

Stand Up for Science celebrated the canceled vote this morning, posting on Bluesky that “people power works.”

It’s unclear whether O’Neill’s nomination has been withdrawn or whether the vote has simply been postponed. Cassidy’s office did not immediately respond to inquiries about O’Neill’s nomination status.

item.title: Wes Moore cautions Dems against shutting down government over Iran war funding
item.description: The Maryland governor told POLITICO that Congress “should be able to” both bring an end to the war and keep the federal government open.

media:content.media:title: POLITICO's Megan Messerly speaks with Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) at the POLITICO Pub during the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah, on Nov. 18, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Aaron Pellish
item.content:encoded:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore expressed frustration at the notion that Congress may shut down the government as Democrats push to tie a funding bill to cutting off Iran war funding.

Moore, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, told POLITICO that while he believes the Trump administration should end the war, the effort by some Democrats to add language to a government funding bill to end the war is misguided.

“I don't know why the American people are being asked to choose between ending a completely rudderless war that we're all paying for and saying, ‘Can we please keep the federal government open?’” Moore said at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah.

“I just think it's incredibly frustrating that once again we are being asked to be in this impossible position to say, 'End a ridiculous war or keep a federal government open,'” he added. “You should be able to do both.”
