When asked if that meant he opposed using the government funding fight to try to force an end to the Trump administration’s military operations against Iran, Moore sharply criticized the Trump administration for launching the “absurd” conflict against Iran.

But the former Army officer who served in Afghanistan cited the importance of keeping the government funded for federal workers who would go without pay during a shutdown, many of whom reside in Maryland.

“As the governor of a state who's going to be impacted more than anybody else, I'm never going to say, ‘Yes, just shut down the government,’” he said. “I think it's ridiculous that Washington even has the ability to do it.”

Some Democrats in both chambers are pressuring leadership to draw a hard line on ending Iran war funding in any stopgap funding bill, which must be passed before the Dec. 11 deadline.

Moore also stressed the importance of keeping the government open in light of recent outages to government systems, including one that triggered a nationwide airplane ground stop last week, and attacked the Trump administration for laying off thousands of federal workers in 2025.

“You cannot separate what is happening with the federal government and these outages with the fact that it's our federal workers who've been fired,” he said.

item.title: Katherine Clark, Pete Aguilar, Joe Neguse elected to House majority posts
item.description: The Democratic leaders all won uncontested races by acclamation.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) speaks during a press conference at 55 M St. SE in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats filled out the top leadership echelon for their incoming majority Wednesday, promoting their current leaders in lockstep as expected.

Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts was elected majority leader, which will make her the first woman to hold the job of floor boss when Democrats take control in January.

Clark ran unopposed and won by acclamation in a closed-door caucus meeting.

House Democrats also elected Rep. Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip and Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker. Both, as with Clark, were unopposed and were elected by acclamation.

The leaders will work with the newly elected caucus chair, Rep. Ted Lieu of California, as well as speaker nominee Hakeem Jeffries of New York. All five have held similar leadership posts in the minority over the past four years.

The group is aligned in pursuing early votes on affordability and mounting aggressive oversight of President Donald Trump and his administration.

item.title: Another rule vote pulled
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
House GOP leaders have canceled a planned Wednesday vote to send two Republican-sponsored bills to the floor due to attendance issues, according to three people granted anonymity to describe internal decisionmaking.

The vote could be rescheduled for later in the week, but it puts passage of two labor-regulations bills — the American Franchise Act and the Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act — into doubt and reflects ongoing difficulties managing the thin GOP majority even after Election Day.

item.title: Trump’s FCC pick advances despite Democratic boycott
item.description: Democratic Senate Commerce Committee members skipped the vote in an attempt to protest Danielle Thumann Severs’ nomination.

media:content.media:title: The Senate Commerce Committee leaders have been at odds over advancing President Donald Trump's FCC nominee.

item.dc:creator: By John Hendel
item.content:encoded:
Senate Commerce Committee Republicans on Wednesday advanced President Donald Trump’s pick to fill an open Federal Communications Commission seat despite a Democratic boycott meant to obstruct the session.

The vote boosts the likelihood that Republicans confirm Danielle Thumann Severs in the lame duck while the party still controls the chamber. That confirmation would cement a deeper Republican majority at the telecom regulator and reduce the need for Trump to compromise and nominate Democrats next year.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called Democrats’ “temper tantrum” Wednesday a “terrible harbinger” heading into the new Congress.

Democrats view the nomination vote as a broader fight for the future of the five-member FCC, which typically is supposed to have members from both parties. But Democrats fear Trump could fire Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat, if he is able to add Thumann Severs to the FCC since it would still have a quorum.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Senate Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) said in a statement before the 10 a.m. scheduled start time.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr currently holds a 2-1 GOP majority, and he requires at least three members for a quorum to conduct much of the FCC's business.

“We made clear to Chairman Cruz that we had concerns about the nominee for the Federal Communications Commission being on the Executive Session until a Democratic nominee is put forward and asked that she be pulled from the markup,” Cantwell added. “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times. This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Cruz said the administration has recently made clear it will move Democratic nominees and maintained Republicans are still in the right to move nominations before them now.

Democrats also worry that Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to Carr, won’t be an independent voice on the commission. Carr has faced particularly intense criticism for how he has threatened and investigated media companies, including this year threatening the eight ABC station licenses of Disney and his scrutiny of TV hosts like Jimmy Kimmel.

item.title: Democrats overwhelmingly nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
item.description: He received an overwhelming, but not unanimous, endorsement from the incoming majority.

media:content.media:title: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 17, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York secured his fellow Democrats’ nomination Wednesday to lead the House, putting him on track to be elected the first Black speaker in January.

Jeffries, who has served in the House since 2013 and as minority leader since 2023, won the uncontested secret ballot 251-11 — an overwhelming, but not unanimous, endorsement from the incoming majority.

While some incoming members withheld their support, he chipped away at skeptics in private meetings and public policy commitments. His candidacy was buoyed by Democrats’ massive midterm victories that delivered a majority that could reach 260 seats once all votes are counted.

Several lawmakers representing different wings of the caucus spoke in favor of Jeffries before the vote, including progressive Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett from a New Jersey swing district and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina — previously the highest-ranking Black House Democrat before Jeffries’ ascension.

In his pitch to members, Jeffries, 56, leaned heavily on his record during two terms as party leader, highlighting Democrats’ resolve during shutdown fights and their success cornering Republicans through procedural maneuvers.

Progressives are enthused that Jeffries this week embraced lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding coverage to include vision, dental and hearing benefits, as well as establishing universal health coverage for children. Centrists have long backed Jeffries, cheering him as a pragmatic, consensus-oriented leader.

Some of the 11 holdouts issued a joint statement Wednesday acknowledging ongoing "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries but adding "there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership."

The group of seven incoming members includes several self-identified democratic socialists, including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Melat Kiros of Colorado and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues," they said.

Jeffries has previewed that early votes under his leadership will include ending President Donald Trump’s tariffs, clawing back Republican-led Medicaid cuts and restoring expired Affordable Care Act tax credits.

He has also emphasized an oversight agenda that targets Trump, his administration and his allies, as well as anti-corruption measures such as a congressional stock trading ban.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this port misidentified Rebecca Bennett's home state. She is from New Jersey.

item.title: Ted Lieu is elected House Democratic Caucus chair
item.description: He is set to be the highest-ranking Asian American House member ever.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) speaks while Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries watches during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ted Lieu of California was elected House Democratic Caucus chair Wednesday morning in a closed-door meeting — the first of numerous leadership elections set to be decided this week.

Lieu, 57, won by acclamation in an uncontested bid for the post, meaning no official vote was tallied. He moves up from caucus vice chair and is now positioned to be the highest-ranking Asian American House member ever.

House Democrats will vote next on a nomination for speaker, where Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is uncontested, followed by elections for majority leader, whip and numerous junior caucus positions.

item.title: Bipartisan Senate duo urges ‘immediate’ White House action on AI-enabled cyber threats
item.description: Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds want leaders to harness existing federal agencies to counter major disruptions.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 8, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds called on the White House Tuesday night to “take immediate action” to protect against intensifying artificial-intelligence-juiced cyber threats against the nation’s infrastructure, financial institutions and software.

The bipartisan duo sent a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, chair of the recently formed “Superintelligence Task Force,” urging him to quickly bring together developers and federal experts to fully use the administration’s tools to counter cyber attacks plaguing banks and other systems.

“AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” wrote Cantwell of Washington, the top Democrat on Senate Commerce Committee, and Rounds of South Dakota, the chair of the Armed Services cybersecurity subcommittee. “We cannot meet these threats with yesterday's cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.”

A spokesperson for Clayton did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new letter comes as the world faces credible threats of AI-enabled hacking targeting bank accounts and highly trafficked websites, jeopardizing personal and financial information worldwide.

Members of Congress are trying to figure out what to do about it, and the senators want Trump administration officials to use existing federal agencies and departments to fend off harm from models going rogue.

The letter urges the White House to direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to craft security standards for defensive AI agents and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to accelerate their adoption at banks, hospitals, utilities and government agencies.

The senators said the expertise within the federal government exists but that a coordinated approach is absent.

“The United States has the technological expertise to lead this effort,” the senators wrote. “What is missing is a coordinated national strategy to bring these capabilities together, establish common security standards, and put effective defenses into widespread use.”

As likely Commerce chair next year, Cantwell will have a new perch to push the administration and conduct oversight as she sees fit. Last month, she released a comprehensive framework that aims to tackle catastrophic risk and other problems.

item.title: Garcia gives Trump allies early warning on the investigations to come
item.description: Democrats plan to use their new power to investigate the White House’s role in the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and Trump family business dealings.

media:content.media:title: House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 23, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.dc:contributor: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats are signaling their top investigative targets in the new Congress, starting with President Donald Trump’s family members and closest aides — from sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump to chief of staff Stephen Miller, former chief Susie Wiles and Vice President JD Vance.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to be the next chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, sent letters to all five Wednesday morning, indicating they will be subjects of interest to the panel next year as he prepares to make good on his promise to probe Trump family business ties, ICE’s mass deportation campaign, the administration’s handling of the Epstein files and more.

The California Democrat sent a total of 12 letters to high-profile figures in Trump’s orbit, including Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner, Attorney General Todd Blanche and former ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, as well as former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her former adviser Corey Lewandowski. The letters, which have no legal force, urge the recipients to preserve documents in anticipation of the investigations Democrats plan to launch when they take over the House in January. And they provide the clearest early window into the soon-to-be-majority’s most pressing investigative priorities.

It’s a sign the incoming Democratic majority will not shy away from confrontations with the White House that could lead to court battles likely to drag on for the remainder of Trump’s term. Administrations of both parties have typically treated senior White House officials — especially chiefs of staff like Miller and Wiles — as immune from compelled testimony to Congress.

The letters are an answer to the Trump administration’s recent warnings about potential criminal prosecution of Democrats who engage in oversight activities it considers “weaponized” or overly punitive.

The White House and Justice Department also have repeatedly warned of possible criminal investigations for demands they consider out of bounds — or lacking a “legitimate legislative task,” as longstanding precedents require. Garcia’s 12 letters nod to that requirement, each including a line describing the investigations as “essential for legislative reform.”

“As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Though some letters request responses by December, Democrats don’t yet have the power to compel answers. And even when they do, congressional oversight requests — including subpoena deadlines — are typically flexible and depend on the targets’ willingness to negotiate and cooperate.

Here’s what Oversight Committee Democrats are most interested in pursuing come January:

Trump family business dealings

Garcia is signaling that Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump will be the subjects of an inquiry into their roles as co-founders of World Liberty Financial, a Trump family cryptocurrency business. The committee’s top Democrat describes the brothers as key players in “the Trump family’s pay-to-play schemes” which “have raked in billions of dollars for the Trump family over the past several years.” A World Liberty Financial spokesperson has previously said “no one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government” and the company is compliant with all U.S. laws.

Donald Trump Jr. is also under scrutiny in connection with his elaborate wedding celebration that was funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with ties to President Vladimir Putin. Kremlev has said the younger Trump paid him back. Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina Trump wrote in a social media post that the celebration was an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend” that had been “recast as something political or sinister.”

“Foreign interests also funded your lavish wedding celebrations, raising further concerns of pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the Trump family,” Garcia said. “These associations may have already benefited special interests, but they have not helped the American people.”

Democrats also have their sights on Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and a U.S. special envoy, for his personal business dealings and government work. Garcia raised concerns that “hundreds of millions of dollars in management fees, business opportunities, and other financial benefits are serving as disguised payoffs for policy changes, preferential treatment, relief from legal scrutiny, and access to sensitive government information and technology.” Kushner has repeatedly denied leveraging his powerful father-in-law for personal gain.

"These allegations have it exactly backwards. Jared Kushner has always acted in the best interests of the United States,” Chad Mizelle, Kushner’s attorney, said. “He has voluntarily stepped away from his successful business to devote his time, without compensation, to helping President Trump end wars, save lives, and advance American interests. Any suggestion that he has used his public service for personal financial gain is categorically false."

The White House has repeatedly denied that Trump or his family members have engaged in any conflicts of interest. The Trump brothers did not immediately return requests for comment.

Garcia also wrote to Catherine Townsend, CEO of the Trust for the National Mall, inquiring about donations by private entities and companies to support Trump’s White House ballroom. Among the companies named is the embattled chip manufacturer Nvidia, which Garcia notes “donated millions to the Trust for the National Mall shortly after receiving permission from the Trump Administration to sell advanced microchips to the People’s Republic of China.”

Nvidia has maintained its donation was made independently of any potential business interests. The Trust for the National Mall said in a statement the organization's "limited role was to receive and manage charitable donations" and "had no role in fundraising or soliciting donations or in design or construction of the project." The organization said it plans to cooperate with congressional inquiries related to the project.

Immigration enforcement

Garcia also outlined the panel’s plans to investigate “the violence, abuse, and corruption carried out by the Department of Homeland Security” under Miller’s direction. The committee said it has found 1,165 instances of concerning uses of force, arrests, deportations and enforcement actions at sensitive locations and other “acts of intimidation or retaliation.”

“Members of the Trump Administration have described you as the ‘linchpin’ and ‘architect’ of the Trump Administration’s most extreme policies, advocating for the widespread abuse of civil liberties,” Garcia wrote to Miller, now Trump’s chief of staff. “We have documented, and will continue to document, your role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending these abuses.”

Garcia also pledged to investigate allegations that Noem “abused DHS funds, undermined career employees, circumvented established safeguards that prevent corruption, and used your position to enrich yourself and associates of the Trump Administration.”

The letter to Noem also makes note of her role running an agency that presided over “pay-to-play schemes conducted” by Lewandowski, her former employee at DHS who is also being probed by the committee for alleged kickbacks from GEO Group, a company that runs private detention facilities for migrants. Lewandowski has previously denied demanding payments from the company.

“Congressman Garcia’s attempts to build a misleading narrative about Mr. Lewandowski as part of his party’s campaign against the current administration will be proven false at the appropriate time and in the appropriate forum,” a spokesperson for Lewandowski said.

Noem was forced out of DHS in March after facing intense scrutiny inside the White House and calls from some GOP lawmakers to resign over her management of the department.

Noem did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Epstein files

Garcia is also probing the administration’s handling of the investigative materials related to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the web of people and institutions who allegedly aided his crimes.

In a letter to Vance, Garcia asked the vice president to identify every meeting officials had on the Epstein files, citing reports outlining Vance’s role in the conversations. Garcia is also seeking information related to the administration’s response to the law Congress passed last year mandating the files’ public disclosure, which lawmakers in both parties have panned as incomplete.

Justice Department officials have said they did their best to follow the law’s disclosure requirements and have sought to correct any errors or address victims’ concerns, but Democrats are still clamoring for sworn testimony from Blanche, who had a key role in overseeing the files’ release.

Garcia is also demanding information about the decision to move Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein's co-conspirator, to a lower security federal prison where she’s serving a 20-year sentence.

He wrote to Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William Marshall III as well as to Tanisha Hall — the warden of Federal Prison Camp Bryan who runs the minimum security facility where Maxwell was moved — to get answers about Maxwell’s transfer after the Justice Department and the Bureau of Prisons “failed to meaningfully respond to any of our inquiries.”

Marshall and Hall did not immediately return requests for comment.

Garcia is, in addition, asking Wiles — Trump’s former chief of staff — and Blanche for information related to the Epstein saga. Wiles was also unreachable for comment.

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.
